title: Why You Should Be Ready for the Retail Buyer Meeting Long Before the Room
summary: Retail buyer meeting readiness turns a defensive conversation into a strategic one. See what changes when operations hold up before you walk in.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


-


Why most buyer-meeting advice stops at avoiding embarrassment


-


What a reactive meeting and a prepared meeting sound like, side by side


-


The operational questions a buyer asks once the product case is settled


---


Most advice about how to be ready for a retail buyer meeting sounds definitive. The standard guidance is to master the financials, bring samples, know the retailer's process, and respect the buyer's time. That advice is sound, but it is also only half the story.


Sooner or later, a buyer will ask an operational question, such as what the fill rate is with current retailers, how many chargebacks landed last quarter, or when the company can send an[advance ship notice](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/edi-856-ship-notice-manifest) (ASN). A supplier who has to go find the answers to these questions spends the rest of the hour explaining, whereas a supplier who answers from memory spends the rest of the meeting time on volume, timing, and how the retailer relationship will develop going forward.


That is the return on operational preparation: The work a supplier does before the meeting decides how much of the meeting is left for growth.


**Related Reading:**[Retail Buyer Meeting Dos and Don’ts](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/retail-buyer-meeting-dos-and-donts)


## What Does Readiness Get You in a Buyer Meeting?


A buyer meeting has two halves.


The first is the product case: margin, velocity, packaging, and the story behind the brand. The second half is operational: Can this company take an order electronically, ship it complete and on time, and account for its own performance history?


Most preparation advice treats that second half as a hazard to survive, but it is better understood as a gate. The product gets a supplier into the room, and operational credibility decides how much of the hour is left for talking about growth.


A supplier who answers the operational questions without hedging has time to talk about the purchase orders (PO), product categories, and store counts. A supplier who can't spends that time promising to follow up. That wasted time defines the difference between a supplier who is prepared for the meeting, and one that is reactive.


## What Does a Reactive Buyer Meeting Look Like?


Picture the founder of a growing food brand presenting to a national grocer. The product case lands well, but then the buyer asks a routine question: What is your fill rate with your current retailers, and how many chargebacks did you take last quarter?


The supplier does not know. The numbers aren’t tracked in a single accessible place; instead, they live in a mix of retailer portals and old email threads. Something in the meeting shifts after this moment: The buyer has learned how the company runs.


### The Supplier Is Often the Last To Know


This gap is rarely carelessness but instead is a reporting problem. In an[Inbound Logistics roundtable on supplier compliance](https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/supplier-compliance-ask-the-experts/) , Greg Holder of Compliance Networks explained that without automated notification, a supply chain failure gets solved inside the retailer's distribution center and never gets reported back to the supplier. A supplier can be missing requirements for months and have no way to find out about it..


The[True Brands case study](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/case-study-true-brands) shows the same pattern from the supplier side. Before the company automated its fulfillment, retailers would surface a chargeback months after a shipment. With no way to trace the activity behind the order, the team often paid the fee without knowing whether it had made the error at all. True Brands also switched providers after its previous[electronic data interchange (EDI)](https://www.spscommerce.com/what-is-edi/) vendor failed testing with several of its major retail customers. vendor failed testing with several of its major retail customers.


## What Changes When the Supplier Is Prepared?


Picture the same growing food brand as before. This time they have a prepared answer for the fill-rate question, as well as the follow-up about chargebacks. The supplier can name the number, the two requirements that caused the most trouble last year, and describe what changed.


As a result, the buyer's next question is different. Rather than getting stuck on metrics, they move toward volume, timing, and which stores to start with.


That shift comes from infrastructure that was in place before the meeting was booked. Take[Jonny Pops](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/jonny-pops-case-study) , for example. When the founders expanded their frozen treats from Twin Cities farmers markets to national distribution, Costco asked them to do EDI as part of the new trading relationship. Readiness was the condition of the relationship, not a refinement that came later.


**Related Reading:**[How to Improve Your Relationship with Your Buyer](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/how-to-improve-your-relationship-with-your-buyer)


## The Importance of EDI Compliance for New Suppliers


EDI is the standard format trading partners use to exchange business documents: the PO the retailer sends, the ASN the supplier sends back, and the invoice that follows. Retailers enforce their own rules on top of that format, covering labeling, timing, and the accuracy of each document. EDI errors produce a deduction from retailers, which is a fee deducted from what the retailer owes.


EDI compliance for new suppliers matters in a buyer meeting because the retailer is deciding whether this relationship will cost its team extra work. Every concrete answer a supplier can give in the meeting is evidence that it will not.


### A Short Supplier Onboarding Readiness Checklist


Many buyers work from a version of the following list:


-


Current fill rate and on-time delivery rate, by retailer


-


Chargeback volume and the specific requirements behind it


-


Whether the company can send and receive EDI documents today


-


Who handles an exception when a shipment goes wrong, and how fast


-


Item data accuracy, including dimensions, weights, and packaging detail


None of these questions are about the product itself; all of them are about the risk the retailer would be taking on.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is retail buyer meeting readiness?


It is the operational prep behind a buyer meeting: A supplier that knows its fill rate, its chargeback history, and its EDI status well enough to answer without looking them up.


### How soon before a buyer meeting should a supplier get EDI capable?


Earlier is better. Many retailers treat EDI as a condition of the trading relationship, not a later step. Suppliers who wait until a retailer asks could end up haggling over a timeline instead of discussing operational capability.


### What do buyers actually ask about compliance?


Most questions come back to fill rate, on-time delivery, chargeback volume, and item data accuracy. The wording varies by retailer, but the question under all of them is whether this supplier will create extra work for the retailer.


### Does a small supplier need all of this before the first meeting?


Not all of it. What matters at a first meeting is knowing where you stand and saying it plainly, including the parts still in progress.
